title: AI Maintenance Software: How It Goes Beyond the CMMS
summary: AI maintenance software detects developing faults from sensor data and drafts the work order. How it differs from a CMMS and why multimodal matters.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- A CMMS records and schedules work after a person spots a problem or a calendar says a task is due. AI maintenance software adds the detection step: sensors on the asset flag a developing fault and draft the work order.
- Multimodal monitoring reads vibration, current, temperature, and acoustic signals on the same asset, so faults that show up first in one signal, such as a motor electrical fault visible in current before vibration changes, can be caught earlier.
- AI does not replace the CMMS. The CMMS still holds asset history, parts, labor, and PM schedules; the AI layer decides which work orders should exist and how urgent they are, and a person still approves and does the repair.


In most plants, maintenance software is a record-keeping system. A technician on rounds hears a pump running rough, someone submits a request, a planner opens a work order, and the CMMS tracks it until it closes.


AI maintenance software changes where the work order comes from. Sensors on motors, pumps, compressors, and fans report continuously. Models compare the signals against each asset's baseline and known fault signatures, and when a fault starts developing, the system drafts a work order naming the asset, the probable fault, and the urgency. A planner reviews it and a technician does the repair, often well before anyone on rounds would have heard the noise.


## What Traditional CMMS Does (and Where It Breaks Down)


A CMMS manages maintenance work: the asset registry, work orders, preventive maintenance schedules, spare parts, and labor history. It breaks down at detection, because it only learns about a problem once a person enters it or a calendar triggers a task.


That design fits reactive and planned[industrial maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-maintenance) well. It leaves three gaps.


### It depends on human detection


Route-based inspections happen weekly or monthly. A bearing defect that starts the day after a route has weeks to progress before the next one, and many early faults make no sound a person can hear on a noisy floor.


### Calendar PMs do not match asset condition


Time-based PMs replace parts on a schedule, whether or not they are worn. The same schedule can miss the gearbox that is degrading faster than its interval assumes, because of a heavier load or a lubricant change.


### Slow-developing failures stay invisible


Lubrication starvation, misalignment introduced during a motor swap, winding insulation breakdown, and cavitation eroding a pump impeller each change the asset's signals well before failure. A CMMS records the[equipment failure](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/equipment-failure) after it happens, often as "replaced bearing" with no root cause, so the history it builds is thin exactly where planners need it.


## What AI Added: Detection Before the Work Order


AI added a detection layer that runs continuously on sensor data and creates a work order when a fault starts developing, before anyone files a request. The work order arrives with the asset, the suspected fault, the evidence behind it, and a suggested priority.


This is[industrial AI](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-ai) , and more specifically[physical AI](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/physical-ai) : models that work from signals measured on real machines. The software learns what normal looks like for each asset at its usual speeds and loads, then flags changes that match known fault patterns, such as a rise in energy at a bearing's defect frequencies or sidebands in motor current.


### What an AI-generated work order looks like


Take a supply fan with a developing outer race defect. Vibration sensors pick up a rise at the bearing's outer race frequency; temperature at the bearing housing starts to creep.


The system classifies it as an early-stage bearing defect, opens a work order for the fan, attaches the trend, and suggests inspecting lubrication now and planning a bearing replacement at the next scheduled stop. The planner confirms, orders the bearing at normal lead time, and slots the job into a planned window.


### What changes for maintenance planning


Lead time is what AI gives the planner. With weeks of warning instead of hours, repairs can be batched into planned shutdowns, parts arrive without expedite fees, and the backlog can be ranked by asset risk instead of by who called loudest. This is[predictive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/predictive-maintenance) carried through to the schedule.


AI catches the failure modes in its detection library, on the assets you instrument. Uninstrumented assets and failure modes the models have not learned still depend on inspections and the CMMS.


For the signal-level detail, see[AI fault detection](https://tractian.com/en/blog/ai-fault-detection) .


## Why Multimodal Matters


Different failure modes show up first in different signals, so a system that reads only vibration can miss, or catch late, faults that start in current, temperature, or sound. Multimodal monitoring combines several signal types on the same asset, so the earliest sign of a fault is more likely to be in view.


Vibration is the backbone of[industrial vibration analysis](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-vibration-analysis) , and it is strong for imbalance, misalignment, and looseness. Other faults speak first in other signals:


Fault Signals where it often shows first Why vibration alone can be late


Lubrication starvation in a bearing Ultrasound and temperature


Friction rises before metal damage changes vibration amplitude


Broken rotor bars or stator winding faults Motor current and magnetic field


Electrical faults change current signature before they produce mechanical vibration


Cavitation in a centrifugal pump Acoustic and high-frequency signals, motor current fluctuation


Broadband noise can be masked in standard vibration bands


Imbalance and misalignment Vibration at 1x and 2x running speed, coupling temperature


Vibration usually catches these well; temperature helps confirm


Overload or process upset Current and temperature


The machine can run smoothly while drawing excess load


A second benefit is confirmation. A temperature rise with no change in vibration or current may be ambient heat on a summer afternoon; a temperature rise paired with a current shift is worth a work order. Cross-checking signals can cut alerts a technician would otherwise walk out to verify for nothing.


At Tractian, multimodal monitoring combines multiple signal types into one unified view of asset health. Within a single sensor, the Smart Trac Ultra reads ultrasound, vibration, temperature, and magnetic field, and the platform combines those signals with context such as OEM documentation and CMMS asset history. The aim is to protect the whole asset, not one component of it, by catching the fault in whichever signal moves first.


## How AI Maintenance Software Works End-to-End


AI maintenance software runs in five steps: sensors capture signals, signal fusion combines them with asset context, fault classification names the likely fault and severity, a prioritized work order is created, and the maintenance team inspects, repairs, and closes it. That last step feeds the model.


1. Sensor.[Industrial IoT sensors](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-iot-sensors) mounted on the asset sample vibration, temperature, current, and sound. A gateway relays the data off the floor; in Tractian's setup it travels over 4G/LTE to the cloud, where the AI analysis runs, so no plant network connection is needed.[Edge AI for industrial plants](https://tractian.com/en/blog/edge-ai-industrial-plants) compares edge and cloud designs.
2. **Signal fusion.** The platform aligns the signals in time and adds context: asset type, running speed, load, bearing model, and maintenance history.
3. **Fault classification.** Models compare features such as RMS, kurtosis, and spectral peaks against the asset's baseline and known fault signatures, then label the likely fault (for example, misalignment) and estimate severity.
4. **Prioritized work order.** The alert becomes a draft work order in the maintenance system, ranked by fault severity and asset criticality, with the evidence attached.
5. **Maintenance team.** A planner approves and schedules it; a technician inspects and repairs. What they find (fault confirmed, root cause, parts used) goes back into the record and helps the models tell real faults from noise next time.


People stay in the loop at steps 4 and 5. The software decides what deserves attention; the team decides what to do about it.


For a full walkthrough of the detection side, see[how AI condition monitoring works](https://tractian.com/en/blog/ai-condition-monitoring) .


## CMMS vs AI-Native Maintenance Platform


The core difference is where work starts. In a CMMS, a person or a calendar creates the work order; in an AI-native platform, sensor data can create it, with a person approving. Most plants that adopt AI keep their CMMS and connect the two.


Traditional CMMS AI-native maintenance platform


Primary job Record, schedule, and track maintenance work


Detect developing faults and turn them into prioritized work


Where work orders come from Requests from people, PM calendars


Sensor alerts, plus requests and PM calendars


Main data source Manual entries and work order history


Continuous sensor data plus maintenance history


Developing faults Found on inspection rounds or at failure


Flagged on instrumented assets as signals change


PM approach Time- or usage-based intervals


Condition-based, with intervals as a backstop


Prioritization Planner judgment, asset criticality


Fault severity and asset criticality


Failure history Often thin root-cause detail


Fault evidence attached to the work order


Best fit Work management across the whole asset base


Critical rotating equipment where failures are costly


An AI CMMS, in the way buyers search for it, usually means one of two things: a CMMS with AI features added, such as text-based work order search or auto-filled failure codes, or a monitoring platform that writes work orders into the CMMS. The second changes which jobs reach the backlog; the first speeds up handling of jobs already there.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is AI maintenance software?


AI maintenance software uses machine learning on sensor and maintenance data to find developing equipment faults and turn them into prioritized work. It typically covers detection, diagnosis, and work order creation, and connects to a CMMS for scheduling, parts, and history. The difference from a classic CMMS is that work can start from sensor data instead of a request or a calendar.


### Can AI replace a CMMS?


Not in most plants. A CMMS manages work across the entire asset base: PM schedules, parts inventory, labor, compliance records, and assets with no sensors. AI adds detection and prioritization on the assets you instrument, and the two work best connected, with AI alerts creating work orders inside the CMMS.


### How does AI improve maintenance planning?


AI gives planners lead time. When a bearing defect is flagged weeks before failure, the repair can be scheduled into a planned stop, parts can be ordered at normal lead time, and jobs can be ranked by asset risk. Planners spend less time reacting to breakdowns and more time sequencing work.


### What is multimodal condition monitoring?


Multimodal condition monitoring combines several signal types, such as vibration, current, temperature, and acoustic data, on the same asset. Because faults show up first in different signals, combining them lets a system catch some faults earlier and confirm alerts before a technician is sent out.


### What is an AI CMMS?


The term is used two ways. Some vendors mean a CMMS with AI features, such as automatic failure coding or natural-language search. Others mean an AI monitoring layer that creates and prioritizes work orders inside the CMMS. Ask which one a vendor means before comparing products.


### Does AI maintenance software create work orders automatically?


It can draft them automatically from sensor alerts, with the asset, suspected fault, evidence, and suggested priority filled in. Many teams keep a planner approval step so alerts are reviewed before labor and parts are committed.


### What equipment benefits most from AI maintenance software?


Rotating equipment with known failure modes and real downtime cost benefits most: motors, pumps, compressors, fans, gearboxes, and conveyors. Assets that stop a line when they fail are the usual place to start. Static assets and low-cost redundant equipment are often better served by inspections and calendar PMs.
